idiom_name: JAAS LoginModule/LoginContext with a Configuration (JDK); Spring Security AuthenticationProvider
implementation_notes: The JDK ships the seam as JAAS: the application calls LoginContext.login() and the Configuration names LoginModules; each module implements initialize/login/commit/abort/logout over a Subject and CallbackHandler, performs verification in login(), and attaches Principals and credentials to the Subject only during commit() - the normalized outcome. A failed credential should throw LoginException, while false means this module is ignored by the configured stack. Modern applications use the same seam one layer up: Spring Security's AuthenticationProvider behind an AuthenticationManager (returning an Authentication carrying principal and authorities) or Jakarta Security's IdentityStore. A hand-written interface plus factory is justified only for mechanisms no framework covers.
pitfalls: LoginModule.login() must not retry, delay or lock; attempt policy belongs to the application, and a bad credential should throw LoginException rather than return false (which means this module is ignored).

A LoginContext instantiates modules reflectively, so an injected verifier field or constructor-only dependency breaks the required public no-argument constructor -> create mechanism state from options or a provider configured outside the sketch.
The shared state map inside a JAAS stack must not become a channel for credentials; Subject and its credentials are security-sensitive objects.
JWT/JWS validation must pin the algorithm and check exp/nbf/aud/iss; decoders do not enforce this for you.
